Atlantoxerus.distinguishing_notes: Only co-occurring genus (MDD countries) is Euxerus (isolated Souss population, Morocco). Kryštufek et al. 2016 diagnose Atlantoxerus as the smallest Xerini and the only one with a light spinal stripe (variably visible), metatarsal pads present (absent in Euxerus), rough but not bristly fur (Euxerus bristly), four pairs of nipples (Euxerus 2-3 pairs), upper incisor with traces of a groove (Euxerus ungrooved per Herron & Waterman 2004 / Ellerman 1940), brachyodont cheek teeth (Euxerus strongly hypsodont per Thomas 1909 / Ellerman 1940), P3 always present (Euxerus ~80%). Head-body 160-220 mm vs Euxerus 223-290 mm in most sources (but see Euxerus notes: a 204 mm young-adult value and a dubious Kingdon 1974 300-460 mm range).

Spermophilopsis.distinguishing_notes: Co-occurring genera (Central Asia): Eoglaucomys, Petaurista, Pteromys (have a patagium; Spermophilopsis none), Eutamias and Funambulus (striped; Spermophilopsis plain, no stripes), Sciurus (arboreal, ear tufts in some; Spermophilopsis 'Ear tufts never present', ears reduced to small folds), Marmota, Spermophilus, Urocitellus (ground squirrels). Best separating characters vs Spermophilus/Urocitellus: enormously long claws (>10 mm, Kryštufek; 'Longest claws usually more than 1cm', Ognev), densely haired soles year-round (Ognev contrasts the bare feet of 'Citellus' [= Spermophilus] fulvus: 'The feet of Citellus fulvus ... are bare'), tail less than half head-body, bristly summer pelage, broad interorbital region ('The same cranial characters distinguish Spermophilopsis from Citellus', Ognev). Cheek pouches are NOT a safe separator (conflicting sources).

Epixerus.distinguishing_notes: Hardest pair: Protoxerus (both very large West/Central African forest squirrels). ADW: 'These squirrels are commonly mistaken for their closest relative, Protoxerus stangeri. The species can only be distinguished morphologically by minute differences in their skulls.' Thomas 1909/Ellerman 1940 skull differences: Epixerus skull elongate with long muzzle, slit-like infraorbital foramen, small bullae, reduced toothrows (Protoxerus: muzzle short, foramen large and rounded, bullae large). Externally HMW cites chevron-shaped red/black/gray banding on the tail underside as Epixerus's most striking feature, while Protoxerus stangeri has a tail with black rings (Denys et al. 2025). vs Funisciurus/Paraxerus: much larger (HB 250-310 mm vs <=251 mm), P3 absent (present in Funisciurus/Paraxerus), lower molars basin-shaped (transversely ridged in Funisciurus/Paraxerus). vs Heliosciurus: larger, ears nearly hairless, tail banding mainly on underside (Heliosciurus tails ringed all round). vs Myosciurus: size. vs Euxerus: soft (not spiny) fur, arboreal/forest.

Funisciurus.distinguishing_notes: vs Paraxerus (the hardest pair; both small striped/unstriped tree squirrels with P3 present): Thomas 1909 separates them on dentition and muzzle - Funisciurus 'Lower molars regularly and deeply ridged, without high cusps. Muzzle very long' vs Paraxerus 'Lower molars irregularly ridged, with high cusps. Muzzle not specially elongated'; Ellerman 1940: Funisciurus lower cheekteeth with cusps obsolete and crowns almost flat, rostrum tending to be elongated. Pelage does not separate them (both genera contain striped and unstriped species; Ellerman notes the Funisciurus lemniscatus group is striped 'as in Paraxerus boehmi group'). Geography helps: Thomas 1909 calls Funisciurus 'the representative of Paraxerus in the West African Forest region'. vs Heliosciurus: Heliosciurus usually lacks P3, has basin-shaped lower molars, no baculum, a ringed tail in all species and no lateral stripes; many Funisciurus have flank/dorsal stripes. vs Protoxerus/Epixerus: much smaller; P3 present. vs Myosciurus: much larger (HB >=160 vs <=75 mm). vs Xerini: soft not spiny fur.

Heliosciurus.distinguishing_notes: Sun squirrels: every species has a ringed (annulated) tail (HMW), usually no P3 (Thomas 1909 cheek-teeth 4/4; P3 vestigial/occasional in ruwenzorii and some individuals), no baculum (Pocock via Ellerman), lower molars basin-shaped without transverse ridges (Thomas 1909), back normally unstriped and no lateral stripes. vs Paraxerus and Funisciurus: those have P3, transversely ridged lower molars, a minute baculum, and many species have lateral/dorsal stripes; but some Paraxerus/Funisciurus also have ringed tails (P. cepapi, P. flavovittis, F. congicus, F. substriatus), so tail rings alone do not separate them. P. poensis (formerly Heliosciurus/Aethosciurus) is the closest look-alike: uniformly coloured, tail without coloured rings, P3 present (Denys et al. 2025). vs Protoxerus/Epixerus: smaller; Protoxerus stangeri also has a ringed tail and lacks P3 - separate by size (HB c. 230-310 vs mostly <250) and skull (Protoxerus infraorbital foramen very large and rounded). vs Myosciurus: size. vs Xerini: soft fur, arboreal. Cranial separator from Protoxerus/Epixerus: infraorbital foramen forms at least a short canal in Heliosciurus (Ellerman 1940 key) vs large, round, no canal in Protoxerus.

Protoxerus.distinguishing_notes: vs Epixerus (hardest pair): Protoxerus muzzle short, infraorbital foramen large and rounded, bullae large, toothrows not reduced (Thomas 1909; Ellerman 1940); Epixerus has elongate skull with long muzzle, slit-like foramen, small bullae. ADW warns the two are externally very similar; tail of P. stangeri with black rings (Denys et al. 2025) vs Epixerus with chevron banding on the tail underside (HMW). vs Heliosciurus: larger (HB 228-310), very large rounded infraorbital foramen, P. stangeri belly nearly naked; both can have ringed tails and lack P3, so those do not separate. vs Funisciurus/Paraxerus: much larger; P3 absent in P. stangeri (present in Funisciurus/Paraxerus); lower molars basin-shaped not transversely ridged. vs Myosciurus: size. vs Xerini (Euxerus, Xerus, Geosciurus): soft fur, arboreal, palate not produced behind molars (Thomas 1909).

Genus min/max for Funisciurus, Heliosciurus and Paraxerus are therefore spans of means plus a few ranges and UNDERSTATE true variation; use them only for gross size gaps (Myosciurus 60-75 mm vs all others >100 mm; Protoxerus/Epixerus vs small Paraxerus). Euxerus max 460 comes from a Kingdon 1974 figure quoted in Mammalian Species 748 that is probably total length; the well-supported adult HB range is 223-290 mm. 2) Thomas 1909 and Ellerman 1940 used older generic concepts: Paraxerus poensis, P. lucifer and P. vexillarius were in Sciurus/Heliosciurus (subgenus Aethosciurus); Heliosciurus ruwenzorii was in Sciurus/Aethosciurus; Protoxerus aubinnii was Myrsilus (Allosciurus in Denys et al. 2025); Euxerus and Geosciurus were subgenera of Xerus in Ellerman; Epixerus wilsoni is now a synonym of E. ebii. Species coverage has been mapped to MDD v2.5 names. 3) Dental fractions in Thomas 1909 and Ellerman 1940 are garbled in OCR; they were read from the page images and are marked verbatim:false with a note. 4) Several 'absent' states are inferences from complete descriptions (e.g. ear tufts from 'ears nearly hairless'/'reduced to a rim', Myosciurus tail rings from a uniform tail description) - each is flagged in notes. 5) Conservative two-state entries were used where sources conflict or the character is subjective: Spermophilopsis cheek_pouches (Ognev 1940 and Kryštufek 2016 'absent' vs Ellerman 1940 'present' citing Vinogradov), tail rings of Xerina (banded tail hairs), Epixerus tail banding, snout length of Funisciurus/Epixerus/Euxerus (long but not shrew-like). 6) tail_distichous 'yes' for Euxerus/Xerus/Geosciurus comes from descriptions of a flattened tail with hairs spreading sideways ('distichous' in HMW for Euxerus); this is subjective and arguably not 'strongly' feather-like. 7) Mammals of Africa Vol. III (Kingdon et al. 2013) - the main modern source for Protoxerini - could not be accessed; ear tufts, cheek pouches, hairy soles, incisor grooves and hypsodonty remain unknown for several Protoxerini genera. 8) MDD lists 10 Funisciurus species (incl.
